skills.name: Letter Sounds
skills.learn: Every letter makes a sound.

card.title: Letters make sounds
card.text: Each letter has its own sound. Listen, then say it.

spec: A honeybee flaps its wings about 200 times every second.

skills.name: First Sounds
skills.learn: Words can start with the same sound.

card.title: Listen to the first sound
card.text: Say the word slowly. The first sound you hear is the beginning sound.

skills.name: Rhyming Words
skills.learn: Rhyming words sound the same at the end.

card.title: Words that rhyme
card.text: Rhyming words have the same ending sound. Only the first sound changes.

spec: Frogs do not need to drink with their mouths. They soak up water through their skin.

skills.name: Short Words
skills.learn: Blend three sounds to read a word.
skills.tip: c, a, t: say each sound, then blend them to make cat.

card.title: Blend the sounds
card.text: Say each sound, then push them together fast to make a word.

spec: Cats sleep for most of the day, often 12 to 16 hours.

skills.name: Sight Words
skills.learn: Some words we know just by looking.

card.title: Words we know by sight
card.text: Some words show up a lot. We learn to know them fast, just by looking.

spec: An owl can turn its head about three quarters of the way around.

skills.name: Clap the Beats
skills.learn: Words have beats. Clap them!

card.title: Clap the beats
card.text: Say the word and clap each part. Each clap is one beat, called a syllable.

spec: Butterflies taste their food with their feet.

skills.name: Capitals and Periods
skills.learn: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a period.
skills.tip: We sit. Big letter first, dot at the end.

card.title: How a sentence looks
card.text: Start with a capital letter. End with a period. The word I is always a capital.

spec: Emperor penguin dads keep their egg warm on top of their feet.

skills.name: Listen to a Story
skills.learn: Listen to a story, then answer who, what, or where.
skills.tip: Make a picture in your head while you listen.

card.title: Listen and picture it
card.text: Listen to the whole story. Think: who is in it, what happens, and where.

spec: Elephants can feel faraway rumbles through their feet.

skills.name: Letter Teams
skills.learn: Two letters can team up to make one new sound.

card.title: Two letters, one sound
card.text: Some letters team up. Together they make one new sound.

spec: Sharks grow new teeth all their lives. They can lose thousands of teeth.

skills.name: Magic E
skills.learn: A silent e at the end makes the vowel say its name.
skills.tip: kit + e = kite. The i says its name.

card.title: The silent e
card.text: An e at the end is quiet. It makes the vowel before it say its name.

spec: A snail has thousands of tiny teeth on its tongue.

skills.name: Blends
skills.learn: In a blend, you hear both letter sounds.

card.title: Blend two sounds
card.text: In a blend, two letters sit together and you hear both sounds.

spec: The Sun is a star. It is the closest star to Earth.

skills.name: Sight Words 2
skills.learn: Read tricky words fast by sight.
skills.tip: said does not sound like it looks. Remember it!

card.title: Tricky words
card.text: Some words do not follow the rules. We learn them by heart.

spec: Sea turtles have lived on Earth for more than 100 million years.

skills.name: Opposites
skills.learn: Opposites mean totally different things.

card.title: Opposites
card.text: Opposite words mean the very different thing.

spec: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.

skills.name: Sort It
skills.learn: Things in a group are alike in some way.

card.title: Groups of things
card.text: Find how the things are alike. Then find the one that is not like the others.

spec: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived.

skills.name: Nouns and Verbs
skills.learn: A noun is a person, place, or thing. A verb is an action.

card.title: Naming words and action words
card.text: A noun names a person, place, or thing. A verb tells an action.

spec: Some ants can carry things many times heavier than their own bodies.

skills.name: End Marks
skills.learn: Every sentence ends with a period, question mark, or exclamation mark.

card.title: End marks
card.text: A telling sentence ends with a period. An asking sentence ends with a question mark. A strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark.

spec: Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time.

skills.name: Read a Story
skills.learn: Read, then answer about the characters and the order of events.

card.title: Story order
card.text: Stories happen in order. Words like first, next, and last help you.

spec: A giraffe's tongue can be about 18 inches long.

skills.name: Vowel Teams
skills.learn: Two vowels can team up to make one long vowel sound.

card.title: Vowel teams
card.text: Two letters work together to make one vowel sound.

spec: You see a rainbow when sunlight shines through raindrops.

skills.name: Compound Words
skills.learn: Two small words can join to make one new word.

card.title: Put two words together
card.text: A compound word is two words joined into one.

spec: Young sunflowers turn to follow the Sun across the sky.

skills.name: Same Meaning
skills.learn: Synonyms are words that mean almost the same thing.

card.title: Synonyms
card.text: Different words can mean almost the same thing.

spec: A chameleon can move each eye on its own, so it looks two ways at once.

skills.name: Prefixes
skills.learn: A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning.

card.title: Word beginnings
card.text: un- means not, or undo. re- means again.

spec: Sloths move so slowly that tiny green algae grow in their fur.

skills.name: Word Detective
skills.learn: Other words in the sentence help you find what a new word means.
skills.tip: Read the whole sentence. Look for a clue.

card.title: Use the clues
card.text: When you meet a new word, read the words around it. They give clues.
examples: The enormous whale was bigger than a bus.

spec: Melted rock is called magma underground and lava when it comes out.

skills.name: Describing Words
skills.learn: Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs tell how something is done.

card.title: Describing words
card.text: An adjective tells what kind. An adverb tells how, and often ends in -ly.

spec: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals. They can run about 60 to 70 miles per hour.

skills.name: Tricky Plurals
skills.learn: Some words change in a special way when there is more than one.

card.title: Special plurals
card.text: Most words add -s. Some words change inside instead.

spec: Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in water, if there were a big enough tub.

skills.name: Fix It Up
skills.learn: Check for capital letters and correct spelling.
skills.tip: Names, days, and months start with a capital.

card.title: Check your writing
card.text: Names of people, places, days, and months start with capitals. Check each word's spelling.

spec: Some parrots can learn to say hundreds of words.

skills.name: Read to Learn
skills.learn: Find the main idea, details, and cause and effect.
skills.tip: Main idea = what the whole passage is mostly about.

card.title: Main idea and details
card.text: The main idea is what the text is mostly about. Details tell more. A cause makes something happen.

spec: About 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water.

skills.name: Big Words
skills.learn: Split long words into syllables to read them.
skills.tip: Each syllable has one vowel sound: rab-bit.

card.title: Break big words apart
card.text: Every syllable has one vowel sound. Split between two consonants. After a long vowel, split right after it.

spec: A hippo can hold its breath underwater for about five minutes.

skills.name: Suffixes
skills.learn: A suffix goes at the end of a word and changes its meaning.

card.title: Word endings
card.text: -ful means full of. -less means without. -able means can be. -ly tells how.

spec: Koalas can sleep up to 20 hours a day.

skills.name: Sound-Alike Words
skills.learn: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.

card.title: Same sound, different word
card.text: Homophones sound the same. The spelling tells you the meaning.

spec: The Moon has no wind, so astronaut footprints there can last for millions of years.

skills.name: Sayings
skills.learn: Some sayings do not mean exactly what the words say.
skills.tip: "Raining cats and dogs" means raining very hard.

card.title: What does it really mean?
card.text: An idiom is a saying with a hidden meaning. A simile compares two things using like or as.
examples: a piece of cake = very easy
as busy as a bee = very busy

spec: A bolt of lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.

skills.name: Subject and Verb
skills.learn: The verb must match the subject: one or more than one.

card.title: Make them match
card.text: If the subject is one (he, she, it), the verb usually ends in -s. If it is more than one, it does not.

spec: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.

skills.name: Tricky Past Tense
skills.learn: Some verbs change in a special way for the past.

card.title: Irregular past tense
card.text: Most verbs add -ed. Some verbs change into a new word instead.

spec: Tyrannosaurus rex lived about 66 to 68 million years ago.

skills.name: Quotation Marks
skills.learn: Quotation marks go around the exact words someone says.

card.title: Show who is talking
card.text: Put quotation marks around the exact words. Put a comma before or after them. The end mark goes inside.

spec: Humpback whales sing songs that can last up to 20 minutes.

skills.name: Read Between the Lines
skills.learn: Use clues in the text plus what you know to figure things out.
skills.tip: Clue + what I know = my inference.

card.title: Make an inference
card.text: The writer does not tell you everything. Find the clues and think about what they mean.

spec: Every dog's nose print is different, like a person's fingerprint.

skills.name: Compare and Contrast
skills.learn: Find how two things are alike and how they are different.

card.title: Alike and different
card.text: Compare: how are they the same? Contrast: how are they different?
examples: Both frogs and toads are amphibians.

spec: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it.

skills.name: Latin Roots
skills.learn: A root is the main part of a word. Many English roots come from Latin.
skills.tip: port means carry. A portable TV can be carried.

card.title: Word roots from Latin
card.text: Find the root, then use its meaning to figure out the whole word.

spec: Beavers build dams from sticks and mud, and their front teeth never stop growing.

skills.name: Prefixes and Suffixes
skills.learn: Prefixes go at the start of a word. Suffixes go at the end. Both change the meaning.

card.title: Word parts
card.text: re- means again. un- and dis- mean not. pre- means before. mis- means wrongly. -tion, -ment, and -ness turn words into nouns.
examples: kindness = the state of being kind

spec: A newborn kangaroo, called a joey, is about the size of a jelly bean.

skills.name: Tricky Homophones
skills.learn: Some words sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.

card.title: Pick the right spelling
card.text: If you can say "they are," "it is," or "you are" instead, use the word with the apostrophe.
examples: their = belongs to them; there = a place; they're = they are
its = belongs to it; it's = it is
your = belongs to you; you're = you are

spec: Giant squid and colossal squid have eyes about as big as dinner plates.

skills.name: Similes and Metaphors
skills.learn: Similes and metaphors compare two different things to paint a picture.
skills.tip: Simile: fast like a cheetah. Metaphor: he is a cheetah.

card.title: Comparing two things
card.text: A simile uses like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another thing. Neither one is meant to be true word for word.
examples: Simile: The snow was as white as milk.
Metaphor: The lake was a mirror.
Real meaning: the lake was smooth and shiny.

spec: A peregrine falcon can dive through the air at more than 200 miles per hour.

skills.name: Idioms and Proverbs
skills.learn: An idiom is a saying with a hidden meaning. A proverb is a short saying that gives advice.
skills.tip: "Under the weather" means feeling sick, not standing under clouds.

card.title: Sayings with a real meaning
card.text: The words of an idiom do not mean what they say. A proverb teaches a lesson.
examples: Idiom: hit the books = study hard
Idiom: once in a blue moon = almost never
Proverb: Look before you leap = think before you act

spec: One ladybug can eat thousands of tiny bugs called aphids during its life.

skills.name: Relative Pronouns
skills.learn: Who, whose, which, and that add more information about a noun.

card.title: Linking words
card.text: Use who for people. Use which for things. Use that for people or things. Use whose to show who owns something.
examples: The book, which is red, is mine.
The boy whose dog barks is Leo.

spec: Flamingos are pink because of the color in the tiny shrimp and algae they eat.

skills.name: Commas
skills.learn: Commas help readers pause in the right places.
skills.tip: Lists: owls, bats, and foxes. Starters: Yes, I can.

card.title: Three comma jobs
card.text: Use a comma between items in a list. Use a comma before and, but, or so when it joins two sentences. Use a comma after a starting word like yes, well, or finally.
examples: We saw owls, bats, and foxes.
I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.

spec: Squirrels bury nuts to eat later, and the nuts they forget can grow into new trees.

skills.name: FANBOYS
skills.learn: FANBOYS words join two sentences into one compound sentence.

card.title: Joining sentences
card.text: Put a comma and a FANBOYS word between two complete sentences. Pick the word that fits the meaning.

spec: Wolves live and hunt together in family groups called packs.

skills.name: Theme
skills.learn: The theme is the big lesson a story teaches.
skills.tip: Ask: what did the character learn? That is often the theme.

card.title: Find the lesson
card.text: Look at what the characters do and what happens because of it. The theme is a lesson you could use in your own life.
examples: Story: a slow tortoise keeps going and wins.
Theme: keep going, even if you are slow.

spec: Some giant tortoises can live for more than 100 years.

skills.name: Compare Two Texts
skills.learn: A first-hand account is by someone who was there. A second-hand account is by someone who was not.
skills.tip: I and we are clues that the writer was there.

card.title: First-hand or second-hand?
card.text: A first-hand account tells what the writer saw and felt. A second-hand account gives facts the writer learned from others.
examples: First-hand: "I saw the Moon cover the Sun."
Second-hand: "An eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun."

spec: During a total solar eclipse, the Moon covers the whole Sun, and the sky turns dark for a few minutes.

skills.name: Greek Roots
skills.learn: Many science words are built from Greek roots.
skills.tip: tele means far. A telescope helps you see far away.

card.title: Word roots from Greek
card.text: Break a big word into its roots. Put their meanings together.

spec: Tardigrades are tiny animals, about half a millimeter long, that can survive being dried out for years.

skills.name: Words in Context
skills.learn: Clues in the sentence can tell you what a new word means.
skills.tip: Look for a definition, an example, or a restatement right after the new word.

card.title: Use the clues
card.text: Read the whole sentence. Look for words that explain, give an example, or say the same thing another way.
examples: The desert is arid. It gets very little rain.

spec: Black bears can sleep through the winter for months without eating or drinking.

skills.name: Personification and Hyperbole
skills.learn: Personification gives human actions to things. Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration.
skills.tip: "The wind whispered" is personification. "I waited forever" is hyperbole.

card.title: Not meant word for word
card.text: Personification: a thing acts like a person. Hyperbole: something is stretched way bigger than the truth to make a point.
examples: The leaves danced in the wind.
Real meaning: my bag is very heavy.

spec: Wind happens when air moves from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure.

skills.name: Keep the Tense
skills.learn: Keep your verbs in the same time: past, present, or future.
skills.tip: Mia opened the door and walked in. Both are past.

card.title: Stay in one time
card.text: If a sentence starts in the past, keep the verbs in the past. Only change the tense when the time really changes.
examples: Future: Leo will run and jump.

spec: Cave stalactites grow drip by drip and can take thousands of years to get long.

skills.name: Conjunction Pairs
skills.learn: Some conjunctions work in pairs.
skills.tip: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, not only ... but also

card.title: Words that come in pairs
card.text: Always match the right partners. Neither goes with nor. Either goes with or.
examples: Either Leo or Mia will go.
Neither Sam nor Ben likes spiders.
Both the cat and the dog slept.
Zoe is not only kind but also funny.

spec: A platypus is a mammal, but it lays eggs.

skills.name: Complex Sentences
skills.learn: A complex sentence joins a full sentence with a part that starts with a word like because or when.
skills.tip: Because it rained, we stayed in. Comma after the first part!

card.title: Subordinating conjunctions
card.text: because and since = the reason. although = a surprise or contrast. when = the time. unless = only if not.
examples: We stayed in because it rained.
Although it was cold, Leo wore shorts.
When the bell rang, we lined up.

spec: After a big rain, a saguaro cactus can soak up and store up to about 200 gallons of water.

skills.name: Summarize
skills.learn: A summary tells the most important ideas in a few words.
skills.tip: A good summary covers the whole passage, not just one detail.

card.title: Short and complete
card.text: A summary gives the main idea and key points. It leaves out small details and your own opinions.
examples: Too small: tells one detail only.
Too much: adds things not in the text.
Just right: covers the whole passage.

spec: Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal, up to about a million hairs per square inch.

skills.name: Author's Purpose and View
skills.learn: Authors write to inform, to persuade, or to entertain. They may also share opinions.
skills.tip: A fact can be proven. An opinion tells what someone thinks.

card.title: Why did the author write this?
card.text: Inform = teach facts. Persuade = try to change your mind. Entertain = tell a fun story. Words like best, should, and I think often show an opinion.
examples: Fact: The Pacific is the largest ocean.
Opinion: The ocean is the best place to visit.

spec: The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface.

skills.name: Find the Evidence
skills.learn: Evidence is a sentence from the text that proves an idea.
skills.tip: Ask: does this sentence really prove the claim, or is it just true?

card.title: Prove it with the text
card.text: Read the claim. Then find the sentence that shows it is true. A sentence can be true but still not prove the claim.
examples: Claim: Camels are built for sand.
Evidence: Long eyelashes keep sand out of their eyes.

spec: A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines on its back.

choices.why: There means a place. The nest belongs to the birds.
They're means they are. "They are nest" does not make sense.

items.explain: their means belongs to them. The nest belongs to the birds.
items.hint: Does the nest belong to someone?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? going to the science museum today.

choices.why: Their means belongs to them. Nothing here belongs to anyone.
There means a place. "There going" does not make sense.

items.explain: They're = they are. "They are going to the science museum today."
items.hint: Try saying "they are" in the blank.

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: Please put the box over ?.

choices.why: Their means belongs to them. The sentence needs a place.
They're means they are. "Over they are" does not make sense.

items.explain: there means a place. Over there. Tip: there has the word here inside it.
items.hint: The sentence tells where to put the box.

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: The cat licked ? paw.

choices.why: It's means it is. "The cat licked it is paw" does not make sense.

items.explain: its means belongs to it. The paw belongs to the cat. 🐱
items.hint: Try "it is" in the blank. Does it make sense?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? raining outside, so bring a coat.

choices.why: Its means belongs to it. The sentence needs "it is."

items.explain: It's = it is. "It is raining outside."
items.hint: Try "it is" in the blank.

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: Is this ? blue jacket?

choices.why: You're means you are. "Is this you are blue jacket" does not make sense.

items.explain: your means belongs to you. The jacket belongs to you.
items.hint: Is the sentence about something that belongs to someone?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? the fastest runner in our class!

choices.why: Your means belongs to you. The sentence needs "you are."

items.explain: You're = you are. "You are the fastest runner in our class!"
items.hint: Try "you are" in the blank.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that is spelled correctly.

choices.t: Their going to feed there dog.
choices.why: The first word should be They're, meaning they are. The second should be their, meaning belongs to them.

choices.t: They're going to feed their dog.
There going to feed they're dog.
choices.why: There means a place, and they're means they are. Both are in the wrong spots.

items.explain: They're (they are) going to feed their (belongs to them) dog.
items.hint: Check each word: can you say "they are" instead?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that is a simile.
items.say: Tap the sentence that is a simile.

choices.t: The snow was a white blanket.
choices.why: This says the snow was a blanket, with no like or as. That is a metaphor.
This sentence does not compare two things.

choices.t: The snow was as white as milk.

items.explain: A simile compares using like or as. "The snow was as white as milk."
items.hint: Look for the word like or as.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that is a metaphor.
items.say: Tap the sentence that is a metaphor.

choices.t: The classroom was loud like a zoo.
choices.why: This uses the word like, so it is a simile.

choices.t: The class went to the zoo.
choices.why: This is a real trip. It does not compare two things.

items.explain: A metaphor says one thing is another. The class was not really a zoo. The real meaning is that it was loud and wild.
items.hint: A metaphor compares without like or as.

items.prompt: "Leo ran like a cheetah." What does this really mean?
items.say: Leo ran like a cheetah. What does this really mean?

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Leo is a boy, so he ran on two legs.
Cheetahs are very fast, not slow.

items.explain: The words say Leo ran like a cheetah. The real meaning is that he ran very fast, because cheetahs are very fast.
items.hint: What do you know about how cheetahs run?

items.prompt: "The stars were diamonds in the sky." What does this really mean?
items.say: The stars were diamonds in the sky. What does this really mean?

choices.t: The stars were made of diamonds.
choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Stars are really balls of hot gas.

choices.t: The stars were hard to see.
choices.why: Diamonds shine, so the stars were easy to see.

items.explain: This is a metaphor. The stars were not really diamonds. The real meaning is that they sparkled brightly, like diamonds do. ✨
items.hint: What do diamonds look like?

items.prompt: "The calm lake was a mirror." Is this a simile or a metaphor?
items.say: The calm lake was a mirror. Is this a simile or a metaphor?

choices.why: A simile uses like or as. This sentence does not.

items.explain: It says the lake was a mirror, with no like or as. That is a metaphor. The real meaning: the water was smooth and showed reflections.
items.hint: Look for like or as.

items.prompt: "Ava is as busy as a bee." Is this a simile or a metaphor?
items.say: Ava is as busy as a bee. Is this a simile or a metaphor?

choices.why: A metaphor has no like or as. This sentence uses as.

items.explain: It compares Ava to a bee using as. That is a simile. The real meaning: Ava is very busy. 🐝
items.hint: Look for like or as.

items.prompt: "Kai's bedroom was a pigpen." What does this really mean?
items.say: Kai's bedroom was a pigpen. What does this really mean?

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. There were no real pigs.
A pigpen is messy, so this means the opposite of clean.

items.explain: This metaphor compares the room to a pigpen. There were no pigs. The real meaning is that the room was very messy.
items.hint: What does a pigpen usually look like?

items.prompt: "The kitten's fur was as soft as a cloud." Which two things are compared?
items.say: The kitten's fur was as soft as a cloud. Which two things are compared?

choices.t: the kitten's fur and a cloud

choices.why: The sky is not in the sentence. The fur is compared to a cloud.
Rain is not in the sentence.

items.explain: The simile compares the kitten's fur to a cloud. The real meaning: the fur was very soft.
items.hint: Look at the words on each side of "as soft as."

items.prompt: "Mia told a joke to break the ice." What does break the ice mean?
items.say: Mia told a joke to break the ice. What does break the ice mean?

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. There was no real ice.

choices.t: to help people feel relaxed and start talking

choices.why: The idiom is not about temperature.

items.explain: The words say break the ice, but there is no ice. The real meaning is to help people feel relaxed and start talking.
items.hint: Why would someone tell a joke to a group of new people?

items.prompt: "Leo has a test tomorrow, so he will hit the books." What does this mean?
items.say: Leo has a test tomorrow, so he will hit the books. What does this mean?

choices.t: Leo will hit his books with his hand.
choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Nobody hits real books.

choices.t: Leo will put his books away.
choices.why: The idiom means to use the books, not put them away.

items.explain: Hit the books really means to study hard. The clue is that Leo has a test tomorrow.
items.hint: What do people do before a test?

items.prompt: "Sam stayed home because he felt under the weather." What does this mean?
items.say: Sam stayed home because he felt under the weather. What does this mean?

choices.t: Sam was standing in the rain.
choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Sam was at home.
People do not stay home because they are happy. This idiom is about health.

items.explain: Under the weather really means feeling sick. It has nothing to do with rain or clouds.
items.hint: Why do kids usually stay home from school?

items.prompt: "We eat at that restaurant once in a blue moon." What does this mean?
items.say: We eat at that restaurant once in a blue moon. What does this mean?

choices.t: We eat there only when the Moon is blue.
choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. The idiom is not about the real Moon.
The idiom means the opposite: almost never.

items.explain: Once in a blue moon really means very rarely, almost never.
items.hint: Is a blue Moon something you see a lot?

items.prompt: What does the proverb "Practice makes perfect" teach?
items.say: What does the proverb, practice makes perfect, teach?

choices.t: You should only do things you are already good at.
choices.why: The proverb says the opposite: practice helps you get good.
The proverb says practice is how you get better.

choices.t: Doing something again and again helps you get better.

items.explain: The lesson is that when you practice a lot, you improve.
items.hint: What happens when you practice a skill every day?

items.prompt: What does "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" mean?
items.say: What does, don't count your chickens before they hatch, mean?

choices.t: Don't count on something good until it really happens.

choices.why: That is about real chickens. The proverb gives advice about plans.

choices.t: Always count your eggs every day.
choices.why: The proverb is not about real eggs.

items.explain: Not every egg hatches. The real lesson: do not count on something until it really happens.
items.hint: Does every plan always work out?

items.prompt: What does "Look before you leap" mean?
items.say: What does, look before you leap, mean?

choices.t: Always jump as high as you can.
choices.why: The proverb is not about real jumping. It is about making choices.

choices.t: Close your eyes when you jump.
choices.why: The proverb says to look, not close your eyes.

items.explain: The words say look before you jump. The real lesson: think carefully before you do something.
items.hint: Why is it smart to look first?

items.prompt: What does "The early bird catches the worm" mean?
items.say: What does, the early bird catches the worm, mean?

choices.t: Birds only eat in the morning.
choices.why: That is about real birds. The proverb gives advice to people.
The proverb is not about real worms.

choices.t: People who start early often do well.

items.explain: The real lesson: if you start early, you have a better chance to get what you want.
items.hint: Who gets the worm: the bird that comes first or last?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: The girl ? won the race is my sister.

choices.why: Which is for things. A girl is a person.
Whose shows that something belongs to someone. Nothing belongs to the girl here.

items.explain: Use who for people. The girl who won the race is my sister.
items.hint: Is the girl a person or a thing?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: I have a friend ? dog can do tricks.

choices.why: Who is for a person doing something. Here the dog belongs to the friend.
Which is for things. The sentence needs to show the dog belongs to the friend.

items.explain: Use whose to show belonging. The dog belongs to my friend.
items.hint: Who does the dog belong to?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: The book, ? has a red cover, is on my desk.

choices.why: Who is for people. A book is a thing.
When extra information is set off by commas, use which, not that.

items.explain: Use which for things. When the extra information is set off by commas, use which, not that.
items.hint: Is a book a person or a thing?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: The bike ? I ride to school is blue.

choices.why: Who is for people. A bike is a thing.
Whose shows belonging, like "whose bike." It does not fit here.

items.explain: That can be used for things. The bike that I ride is blue. 🚲
items.hint: A bike is a thing.

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: The scientist ? studies whales visited our class.

choices.why: Which is for things. A scientist is a person.
Whose shows belonging. The sentence tells what the scientist does.

items.explain: Use who for people. The scientist who studies whales visited our class. 🐋
items.hint: Is a scientist a person or a thing?

items.prompt: Which word fits the sentence?
items.visual: A maple is a tree ? leaves turn red in the fall.

choices.why: Who is for people. A tree is not a person.
"A tree which leaves" does not make sense. The leaves belong to the tree.

items.explain: Use whose to show belonging. The leaves belong to the tree. 🍁
items.hint: Whose leaves? The tree's leaves.

items.prompt: Tap the relative pronoun in this sentence.
items.visual: The frog that lives in our pond is green.

choices.why: Frog is a noun. It names the animal.
Pond is a noun. It names a place.

items.explain: That is the relative pronoun. It starts the part "that lives in our pond," which tells more about the frog. 🐸
items.hint: Look for who, whose, which, or that.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with commas in the right places.

choices.t: We saw owls, bats, and foxes.
We saw, owls bats and foxes.
choices.why: The comma should not go after saw. Commas go between the items in the list.

choices.t: We saw owls bats, and foxes.
choices.why: A comma is missing between owls and bats.

items.explain: In a list, put a comma after each item before and: owls, bats, and foxes.
items.hint: Put a comma between each thing in the list.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.t: I wanted to swim but, the pool was closed.
choices.why: The comma goes before but, not after it.

choices.t: I wanted, to swim but the pool was closed.
choices.why: The comma should not split "wanted to swim."

choices.t: I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.

items.explain: Two sentences are joined by but. Put the comma before but.
items.hint: Find the joining word. The comma goes just before it.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.why: The comma goes right after the starting word Yes.
The comma should not split "will help."

items.explain: Put a comma after a starting word like yes, no, or well.
items.hint: Where would you pause after the first word?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.t: Well, I think it will rain today.
Well I, think it will rain today.
choices.why: The comma goes right after the starting word Well.

choices.t: Well I think it, will rain today.
choices.why: This comma splits the sentence in the wrong place.

items.explain: Well is a starting word. Put a comma right after it.
items.hint: Pause after the first word.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.t: It was cold so, Zoe wore a hat.
choices.why: The comma goes before so, not after it.

choices.t: It was cold, so Zoe wore a hat.

items.explain: "It was cold" and "Zoe wore a hat" are two sentences joined by so. The comma goes before so.
items.hint: The comma goes before the joining word.

items.prompt: Why does this sentence need a comma?
items.visual: Finally, the rain stopped.

choices.t: It separates items in a list.
choices.why: There is no list in this sentence.
There is only one sentence here. There is no joining word like and or but.

choices.t: It comes after a starting word.

items.explain: Finally is a starting word, so a comma comes after it.
items.hint: Look at the first word.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with commas in the right places.

choices.t: The puppy jumped ran, and barked.
choices.why: A comma is missing after jumped.

choices.t: The puppy, jumped, ran, and barked.
choices.why: Do not put a comma between the puppy and its first action.

choices.t: The puppy jumped, ran, and barked.

items.explain: This is a list of actions: jumped, ran, and barked.
items.hint: Commas go between the actions in the list.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.why: The comma goes right after the starting word Oh.
This comma splits "look at that rainbow."

items.explain: Oh is a starting word. Put a comma right after it. 🌈
items.hint: Pause after the first word.

items.prompt: Which word best joins the two parts?
items.visual: I was hungry, ? I ate an apple.

choices.why: But shows a difference. Eating because you are hungry is not a difference.
Or shows a choice. There is no choice here.

items.explain: so shows a result. I was hungry, so I ate. 🍎
items.hint: Eating is the result of being hungry.

items.prompt: Which word best joins the two parts?
items.visual: Leo wanted to play outside, ? it was raining.

choices.why: So shows a result. Rain is not a reason to go play outside.
For means because. Rain is not the reason Leo wanted to play.

items.explain: but shows a difference. Leo wanted to play, but the rain got in the way.
items.hint: Do the two parts go together, or do they clash?

items.prompt: Which word best joins the two parts?
items.visual: Do you want milk, ? do you want juice?

choices.why: So shows a result. This question asks you to choose.
Yet shows a difference. This question asks you to choose.

items.explain: or shows a choice: milk or juice.
items.hint: The question gives two choices.

items.prompt: Which word is a FANBOYS conjunction?
items.say: Which word is a fan boys conjunction?

choices.why: Because is a joining word, but it is not one of the FANBOYS.
When is a joining word, but it is not one of the FANBOYS.

items.explain: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. Yet is the Y.
items.hint: Say the letters: F, A, N, B, O, Y, S.

items.prompt: Tap the compound sentence.

choices.t: The sun set over the hills.
choices.why: This is one sentence with one subject and one verb.

choices.t: The sun set, and the stars came out.
The sun and the stars shine.
choices.why: This has two subjects but only one verb, so it is one simple sentence.

items.explain: "The sun set" and "the stars came out" are two sentences joined by , and. That makes a compound sentence. ⭐
items.hint: Look for two full sentences joined by a FANBOYS word.

items.prompt: Which sentence best joins "Ava studied hard" and "She passed the test"?
items.say: Which sentence best joins, Ava studied hard, and, she passed the test?

choices.t: Ava studied hard, but she passed the test.
choices.why: But shows a difference. Passing is not a surprise after studying.

choices.t: Ava studied hard, or she passed the test.
choices.why: Or shows a choice. Ava did both things.

choices.t: Ava studied hard, so she passed the test.

items.explain: Passing the test was the result of studying, so use so.
items.hint: Which part happened because of the other?

items.prompt: In this sentence, what does for mean?
items.say: In this sentence, what does for mean?
items.visual: Mia wore her warm coat, for it was very cold.

choices.why: But shows a difference. The cold is the reason for the coat.
Or shows a choice. There is no choice here.

items.explain: Here for means because. Mia wore her coat because it was cold.
items.hint: Why did Mia wear her coat?

items.prompt: Which word best joins the two parts?
items.visual: Noah does not like peas, ? does he like carrots.

choices.why: "And does he like carrots" does not fit. Use nor to add another "not."
So shows a result. Not liking peas does not cause not liking carrots.

items.explain: nor adds another "not." Noah does not like peas, nor does he like carrots.
items.hint: Both parts say what Noah does not like.

items.prompt: What is the theme of this fable?
items.visual: A hare bragged that he was much faster than the tortoise. They agreed to race to the big oak tree. The hare ran far ahead, then lay down for a nap. The tortoise kept walking, one slow step at a time. When the hare woke up, the tortoise was already at the tree.

choices.why: That is a fact from the story, not the lesson. Also, the hare lost.

choices.t: Keep going, even if you are slow.

choices.why: The nap is the reason the hare lost.

items.explain: Clue: "The tortoise kept walking, one slow step at a time." The tortoise did not stop, so it won. Lesson: keep going.
items.hint: Who won, and what did that character do?

items.prompt: What is the theme of this fable?
items.visual: All summer, the ant carried seeds to its nest. The grasshopper sang and played in the sun. "Why work so hard?" the grasshopper asked. When winter came, snow covered the ground. The ant had plenty of food, but the grasshopper had none. The ant shared, and the grasshopper promised to plan ahead next year.

choices.t: Plan ahead for what you will need later.
Singing is more fun than working.
choices.why: The grasshopper had fun, but then had no food. The story does not praise that choice.

choices.t: Snow covers the ground in winter.
choices.why: That is a detail from the story, not the lesson.

items.explain: Clue: "The grasshopper promised to plan ahead next year." The ant worked early and was ready for winter.
items.hint: What did the grasshopper learn at the end?

items.prompt: What is the theme of this fable?
items.visual: A tiny mouse woke a sleeping lion. The lion could have been angry, but he let the mouse go. Later, the lion got tangled in a rope net. The mouse chewed through the ropes and set the lion free. "You were kind to me, so I helped you," said the mouse.

choices.why: That is a fact about animals, not the lesson of the story.

choices.t: Never go near a rope net.
choices.why: The net is a detail. The story is about kindness.

choices.t: A kind act can come back to you.

items.explain: Clue: "You were kind to me, so I helped you," said the mouse. The lion's kindness came back to him.
items.hint: Read what the mouse says at the end.

items.prompt: What is the theme of this story?
items.visual: Kai wanted to play a song on the piano. At first, he kept hitting the wrong keys. He felt like quitting, but he practiced a little every day. After three weeks, he could play the whole song. At the show, everyone clapped for him.

choices.why: The story does not talk about carrying a piano.

choices.t: Hard work and practice help you improve.
If something is hard, you should stop.
choices.why: Kai felt like quitting, but he kept practicing and did well.

items.explain: Clue: "He felt like quitting, but he practiced a little every day." His practice helped him play the whole song. 🎹
items.hint: What did Kai do after he felt like quitting?

items.prompt: What is the theme of this fable?
items.visual: A thirsty crow found a tall pitcher with a little water at the bottom. Its beak could not reach the water. The crow did not give up. It dropped pebbles into the pitcher, one by one. The water rose higher and higher until the crow could drink.

choices.why: The crow used the pebbles to solve a problem. The story is not about collecting them.

choices.t: Water is found at the bottom of pitchers.
choices.why: That is a detail, not the lesson.

choices.t: Clever thinking can solve a hard problem.

items.explain: Clue: "It dropped pebbles into the pitcher, one by one." The crow used a smart idea to reach the water.
items.hint: How did the crow get a drink?

items.prompt: What is the theme of this story?
items.visual: Omar bumped the table, and his mom's plant fell over. Dirt spilled on the floor. Omar felt nervous, but he told his mom what happened. She hugged him. "Thank you for telling the truth," she said. They cleaned it up together.

choices.t: It is best to tell the truth.
Plants should not go on tables.
choices.why: Where the plant sits is a detail. The story is about Omar telling the truth.
The story does not say how Omar felt about cleaning.

items.explain: Clue: "Thank you for telling the truth," she said. Omar was honest, and it went well.
items.hint: Read what Omar's mom says to him.

items.prompt: What is the theme of this story?
items.visual: Ben, Zoe, and Noah each tried to lift a heavy box of books. Alone, none of them could move it. Then they each grabbed one side. They lifted together, and the box rose off the floor. "That was easy!" said Zoe.

choices.why: That is a detail. The lesson is about how the kids solved the problem.

choices.t: Working together makes hard jobs easier.
It is better to work alone.
choices.why: Alone, none of them could lift the box.

items.explain: Clue: "They lifted together, and the box rose off the floor." Alone they failed. Together it was easy.
items.hint: What changed between trying alone and trying together?

items.prompt: Which sentence from the story best shows the theme?
items.visual: Rosa had two umbrellas on a rainy day. Her classmate Lily had none. Rosa gave one umbrella to Lily. The next week, Rosa forgot her lunch. Lily shared her sandwich. "You helped me, so now I will help you," Lily said.

choices.t: Rosa had two umbrellas on a rainy day.
choices.why: This sets up the story, but it does not show the lesson.

choices.t: The next week, Rosa forgot her lunch.
choices.why: This is a problem in the story, not the lesson.

choices.t: "You helped me, so now I will help you," Lily said.

items.explain: The theme is that kindness comes back to you. Lily's words, "You helped me, so now I will help you," say it directly.
items.hint: Which sentence tells why Lily shared?

items.prompt: Which text is a first-hand account?
items.visual:
Text 1 I put on my eclipse glasses and looked up. Slowly, the Moon covered the Sun. The sky grew dark, and the birds got quiet. I felt a chill, and I held my dad's hand. It was the most amazing thing I have ever seen!
Text 2 A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. The Moon blocks the Sun's light. During a total eclipse, the sky can get dark for a few minutes. People must use special glasses to look at the Sun safely.

choices.why: Text 2 explains facts. The writer does not say they were there.
Only Text 1 uses I and tells what the writer saw and felt.

items.explain: Text 1 says "I put on my eclipse glasses and looked up." The writer was there, so it is a first-hand account.
items.hint: Which text uses the word I?

items.prompt: What does Text 1 tell that Text 2 does not?
items.say: What does Text 1 tell that Text 2 does not?
items.visual:
Text 1 I put on my eclipse glasses and looked up. Slowly, the Moon covered the Sun. The sky grew dark, and the birds got quiet. I felt a chill, and I held my dad's hand. It was the most amazing thing I have ever seen!
Text 2 A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. The Moon blocks the Sun's light. During a total eclipse, the sky can get dark for a few minutes. People must use special glasses to look at the Sun safely.

choices.why: Text 2 explains why an eclipse happens. Text 1 does not.
Both texts talk about eclipse glasses.

choices.t: how the writer felt during the eclipse

items.explain: Only Text 1 tells feelings: "I felt a chill" and "It was the most amazing thing I have ever seen!"
items.hint: Which text tells about feelings?

items.prompt: What does Text 2 explain that Text 1 does not?
items.say: What does Text 2 explain that Text 1 does not?
items.visual:
Text 1 I put on my eclipse glasses and looked up. Slowly, the Moon covered the Sun. The sky grew dark, and the birds got quiet. I felt a chill, and I held my dad's hand. It was the most amazing thing I have ever seen!
Text 2 A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. The Moon blocks the Sun's light. During a total eclipse, the sky can get dark for a few minutes. People must use special glasses to look at the Sun safely.

choices.why: Both texts say the sky gets dark.

choices.t: that the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth

choices.why: Only Text 1 tells about the birds.

items.explain: Text 2 explains the science: "A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth." 🌑
items.hint: Which text explains how an eclipse works?

items.prompt: How are the two texts alike?
items.visual:
Text 1 Our boat rocked on the waves as we looked for whales. Suddenly, a humpback whale leaped out of the water! It landed with a huge splash that sprayed us. Everyone on the boat cheered. I will never forget that day.
Text 2 Humpback whales can grow to about 50 feet long. They often leap out of the water. This leap is called breaching. Scientists are not sure why whales breach. Humpbacks travel thousands of miles each year.

choices.t: Both tell how long humpback whales grow.
choices.why: Only Text 2 tells how long they grow.

choices.t: Both tell about humpback whales leaping out of the water.
Both were written by someone on a boat.
choices.why: Only the writer of Text 1 was on a boat.

items.explain: Text 1: "a humpback whale leaped out of the water." Text 2: "They often leap out of the water." 🐳
items.hint: Find an idea that is in both texts.

items.prompt: Which word from Text 2 names what the whale in Text 1 did?
items.visual:
Text 1 Our boat rocked on the waves as we looked for whales. Suddenly, a humpback whale leaped out of the water! It landed with a huge splash that sprayed us. Everyone on the boat cheered. I will never forget that day.
Text 2 Humpback whales can grow to about 50 feet long. They often leap out of the water. This leap is called breaching. Scientists are not sure why whales breach. Humpbacks travel thousands of miles each year.

choices.why: Traveling means going a long way. The whale in Text 1 leaped.
Growing means getting bigger. The whale in Text 1 leaped.

items.explain: Text 2 says the leap "is called breaching." In Text 1, the whale leaped out of the water, so it was breaching.
items.hint: Text 2 gives a special name for the leap.

items.prompt: Why does Text 1 use the words "I," "we," and "us"?
items.say: Why does Text 1 use the words I, we, and us?
items.visual:
Text 1 Our boat rocked on the waves as we looked for whales. Suddenly, a humpback whale leaped out of the water! It landed with a huge splash that sprayed us. Everyone on the boat cheered. I will never forget that day.
Text 2 Humpback whales can grow to about 50 feet long. They often leap out of the water. This leap is called breaching. Scientists are not sure why whales breach. Humpbacks travel thousands of miles each year.

choices.t: The writer was there and saw it happen.
The writer is a whale scientist.
choices.why: The text never says the writer is a scientist.

choices.t: The writer is giving a list of facts.
choices.why: Text 2 gives facts. Text 1 tells a personal experience.

items.explain: Clue: the splash "sprayed us." The writer was on the boat. That makes Text 1 a first-hand account.
items.hint: Was the writer on the boat?

items.prompt: Which text is a second-hand account?
items.visual:
Text 1 Last fall, my class visited a butterfly garden. Hundreds of orange monarchs rested on the flowers. One landed right on my shoulder! Our guide said they were stopping to eat on a long trip south.
Text 2 Each fall, many monarch butterflies fly south to Mexico. Some fly as far as 3,000 miles. They stop along the way to drink nectar from flowers. In the spring, monarchs head north again.

choices.why: Text 1 is first-hand. The writer says a butterfly "landed right on my shoulder."

items.explain: Text 2 gives facts without saying the writer was there. That makes it a second-hand account.
items.hint: Which text does not use I or my?

items.prompt: What do both texts say about monarchs?
items.say: What do both texts say about monarchs?
items.visual:
Text 1 Last fall, my class visited a butterfly garden. Hundreds of orange monarchs rested on the flowers. One landed right on my shoulder! Our guide said they were stopping to eat on a long trip south.
Text 2 Each fall, many monarch butterflies fly south to Mexico. Some fly as far as 3,000 miles. They stop along the way to drink nectar from flowers. In the spring, monarchs head north again.

choices.t: They fly as far as 3,000 miles.
choices.why: Only Text 2 gives this number.
Only Text 1 tells about a monarch landing on someone.

choices.t: They stop to eat on their trip south.

items.explain: Text 1: "they were stopping to eat on a long trip south." Text 2: "They stop along the way to drink nectar." 🦋
items.hint: Find an idea you can see in Text 1 and in Text 2.

items.prompt: bio means life. -ology means study of. What is biology?
items.say: Bio means life. The ending ology means study of. What is biology?

choices.t: the study of rocks and land
choices.why: That is geology. Geo means earth.
Hydro means water. Bio means life.

items.explain: bio (life) + -ology (study of) = the study of living things. The ending -logy, often seen as -ology, means study of. 🌿
items.hint: Put the two meanings together.

items.prompt: A telescope helps you see stars. What does tele mean?
items.say: A telescope helps you see stars. What does tele mean?

choices.why: Small is the meaning of micro.
Heat is the meaning of therm.

items.explain: tele means far. A telescope helps you see things that are far away. A telephone lets you talk to someone far away. 🔭
items.hint: Are stars close or far away?

items.prompt: therm means heat. What does a thermometer measure?
items.say: Therm means heat. What does a thermometer measure?

choices.why: Weight is measured with a scale. Therm means heat.
Length is measured with a ruler. Therm means heat.

choices.t: how hot or cold something is

items.explain: therm (heat) + meter (measure) = a tool that measures how hot or cold something is. 🌡️
items.hint: What does therm mean?

items.prompt: A scientist wants to see tiny cells. Which tool should she use?
items.say: A scientist wants to see tiny cells. Which tool should she use?

choices.why: Tele means far. A telescope is for things far away, like stars.
Therm means heat. A thermometer measures temperature.

items.explain: micro means small. A microscope helps you see very small things. 🔬
items.hint: Which root means small?

items.prompt: Geography is about Earth's land and places. What does geo mean?
items.say: Geography is about Earth's land and places. What does geo mean?

choices.why: Light is the meaning of photo.
Life is the meaning of bio.

items.explain: geo means earth. geo (earth) + graph (write) = writing about Earth. 🌎
items.hint: Geography studies maps, land, and places on Earth.

items.prompt: Which root means water?
items.say: Which root means water?

choices.why: Photo means light.
Graph means write.

items.explain: hydro means water. A fire hydrant gives water. Hydropower is energy from moving water. 💧
items.hint: Think of a fire hydrant.

items.prompt: photo means light. graph means write. What is a photograph?
items.say: Photo means light. Graph means write. What is a photograph?

choices.why: A letter is written with a pen. Photo means light.
Geo means earth. There is no geo in photograph.

items.explain: photo (light) + graph (write) = "writing with light." A camera uses light to make a picture. 📷
items.hint: Put the two meanings together.

items.prompt: A biography is a book about a real person. Which meaning fits best?
items.say: A biography is a book about a real person. Which meaning fits best?

choices.why: Far is tele and light is photo. Biography has bio and graph.
Tiny is micro. Biography has bio and graph.

items.explain: bio (life) + graph (write) = writing about someone's life.
items.hint: bio = life. graph = write.

items.prompt: What does hibernate mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does hibernate mean in this sentence?
items.visual: Some bears hibernate, sleeping deeply in their dens all winter.

choices.why: The sentence says the bears are sleeping, not hunting.
The bears are in their dens, not in water.

items.explain: Clue: "sleeping deeply in their dens all winter." That restates what hibernate means. 🐻
items.hint: Read the words right after the comma.

items.prompt: What does arid mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does arid mean in this sentence?
items.visual: The desert is arid. It gets less than 10 inches of rain a year.

choices.why: The clue is about rain, not temperature.
Less than 10 inches of rain a year is very little rain.

items.explain: Clue: "It gets less than 10 inches of rain a year." Very little rain means very dry. 🌵
items.hint: Is 10 inches of rain a year a lot or a little?

items.prompt: What does metamorphosis mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does metamorphosis mean in this sentence?
items.visual: During metamorphosis, a caterpillar changes its whole body and becomes a butterfly.

choices.why: The sentence is about the body changing, not about eating.
The sentence does not describe a place.

choices.t: a big change in body form

items.explain: Clue: "a caterpillar changes its whole body and becomes a butterfly." 🐛➡️🦋
items.hint: What happens to the caterpillar?

items.prompt: What does barter mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does barter mean in this sentence?
items.visual: Long ago, people would barter, trading furs for tools instead of using money.

choices.t: to save money in a bank
choices.why: The sentence says "instead of using money."
The tools were traded for, not made.

items.explain: Clue: "trading furs for tools instead of using money." That explains what barter means.
items.hint: Read the words right after the comma.

items.prompt: What does independence mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does independence mean in this sentence?
items.visual: The colonists wanted independence, the freedom to rule themselves.

choices.why: The sentence does not talk about an army.
The sentence does not talk about money.

items.explain: Clue: "the freedom to rule themselves." The words after the comma define independence.
items.hint: Read the words right after the comma.

items.prompt: What does photosynthesis mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does photosynthesis mean in this sentence?
items.visual: Plants use photosynthesis to make their own food from sunlight, water, and air.

choices.t: the way plants drink from rivers
choices.why: The sentence says plants make food, not that they drink from rivers.
The sentence is about making food, not seeds.

choices.t: the way plants make food using sunlight

items.explain: Clue: "to make their own food from sunlight, water, and air." 🌱
items.hint: What do plants make, and what do they use?

items.prompt: What does condense mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does condense mean in this sentence?
items.visual: Water vapor began to condense on the cold glass, forming tiny drops of water.

choices.why: The glass is cold, not hot.

choices.t: to change from a gas into a liquid

choices.why: The sentence says drops of water, not ice.

items.explain: Clue: water vapor (a gas) is "forming tiny drops of water" (a liquid). That is condensing. 💧
items.hint: Water vapor is a gas. What does it turn into?

items.prompt: What does erosion mean in this sentence?
items.say: What does erosion mean in this sentence?
items.visual: Erosion slowly wore away the riverbank as the water carried soil downstream.

choices.t: the wearing away of land by water or wind
the building of a new river
choices.why: The sentence says land was worn away, not built.
The sentence is about soil being carried away, not plants.

items.explain: Clue: "wore away the riverbank as the water carried soil downstream."
items.hint: What happened to the riverbank?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that uses personification.
items.say: Tap the sentence that uses personification.

choices.t: The wind blew hard all night.
choices.why: Wind really blows. This is not a human action.

choices.t: The wind whispered through the trees.
The wind was as cold as ice.
choices.why: This compares with as. It is a simile.

items.explain: Only people can whisper. "The wind whispered" gives the wind a human action. Real meaning: the wind made a soft sound.
items.hint: Which sentence makes the wind act like a person?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that uses hyperbole.
items.say: Tap the sentence that uses hyperbole.

choices.t: I have five things to do today.
choices.why: Five things could really be true. It is not an exaggeration.

choices.t: My to-do list smiled at me.
choices.why: A list smiling is personification, not hyperbole.

choices.t: I have a million things to do today.

items.explain: No one really has a million things to do in one day. It is a huge exaggeration. Real meaning: I have a lot to do.
items.hint: Which sentence stretches the truth way too far?

items.prompt: "My backpack weighs a ton." What does this really mean?
items.say: My backpack weighs a ton. What does this really mean?

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. No kid could carry that.
The saying means the opposite of empty.

items.explain: This is hyperbole. The backpack does not really weigh a ton. The real meaning: it is very heavy.
items.hint: Is the speaker telling the exact weight, or stretching it?

items.prompt: "The sun smiled down on the park." Which kind of language is this?
items.say: The sun smiled down on the park. Which kind of language is this?

choices.why: Hyperbole is a big exaggeration. This gives the sun a human action.

items.explain: The sun cannot really smile. That is a human action, so this is personification. Real meaning: it was bright and sunny. ☀️
items.hint: Can the sun really smile?

items.prompt: "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse." What does this really mean?
items.say: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse. What does this really mean?

choices.t: The speaker wants to eat a horse.
choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. It is a big exaggeration.
The saying means the speaker is very hungry.

items.explain: This is hyperbole. Nobody could really eat a horse. The real meaning: the speaker is very hungry.
items.hint: Why would someone say something so big?

items.prompt: "The old car coughed and groaned up the hill." What does this really mean?
items.say: The old car coughed and groaned up the hill. What does this really mean?

choices.t: The car made rough, noisy sounds.

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Cars cannot get sick.

choices.t: The car went up the hill very fast.
choices.why: Coughing and groaning show the car was struggling, not fast.

items.explain: This is personification. Cars cannot cough or groan like people. The real meaning: the car made rough, noisy sounds.
items.hint: What sounds might an old car make going uphill?

items.prompt: "Leo waited forever for the bus." Which kind of language is this?
items.say: Leo waited forever for the bus. Which kind of language is this?

choices.why: Personification gives a thing human actions. Leo is a person.

items.explain: Leo did not really wait forever. That is an exaggeration, so it is hyperbole. Real meaning: he waited a long time.
items.hint: Can someone really wait forever?

items.prompt: "The flowers danced in the breeze." What does this really mean?
items.say: The flowers danced in the breeze. What does this really mean?

choices.why: That is the word-for-word meaning. Flowers cannot really dance.

choices.t: The flowers swayed back and forth in the wind.
The flowers were pulled out of the ground.
choices.why: The flowers moved in the breeze but stayed in the ground.

items.explain: This is personification. Flowers cannot dance. The real meaning: the wind made them sway back and forth. 🌸
items.hint: What does a breeze do to flowers?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that keeps the same verb tense.

choices.t: Mia opened the door and walks inside.
choices.why: Opened is past, but walks is present.

choices.t: Mia opens the door and walked inside.
choices.why: Opens is present, but walked is past.

choices.t: Mia opened the door and walked inside.

items.explain: Opened and walked are both past tense.
items.hint: Both verbs should be in the same time.

items.prompt: Which verb fits the sentence?
items.visual: Yesterday, Leo ? to the park and played soccer.

choices.why: Goes is present. Yesterday and played show the past.
Will go is future. Yesterday and played show the past.

items.explain: Yesterday and played show the past, so use went.
items.hint: Look at the word Yesterday.

items.prompt: Which verb fits the sentence?
items.visual: Every morning, Ava wakes up and ? her teeth.

choices.why: Brushed is past. Wakes is present, and this happens every morning.
Will brush is future. Wakes is present, and this happens every morning.

items.explain: Wakes is present tense, so use brushes. Things that happen every day use present tense.
items.hint: Match the tense of wakes.

items.prompt: Which verb does not match the others?
items.say: Which verb does not match the others?
items.visual: The squirrel climbed the tree, found an acorn, and eats it.

choices.why: Climbed is past, like found. It matches.
Found is past, like climbed. It matches.

items.explain: Climbed and found are past. Eats is present. It should be ate. 🐿️
items.hint: Two verbs are past. Which one is not?

items.prompt: Which verb fits the sentence?
items.visual: Tomorrow, we will visit the museum and ? the dinosaur bones.

choices.why: Saw is past. Tomorrow and will visit show the future.
Seen needs a helper like have. Tomorrow shows the future.

items.explain: "We will visit ... and (will) see." Both verbs are in the future. 🦖
items.hint: The word will goes with both verbs.

items.prompt: Which sentence fixes the tense mistake?
items.visual: Kai runs to the bus and waved to his friend.

choices.t: Kai runs to the bus and will wave to his friend.
choices.why: Will wave is future, but runs is present. The tenses still do not match.

choices.t: Kai runs to the bus and waves to his friend.
Kai runs to the bus and waving to his friend.
choices.why: Waving needs a helper like is. It is not a complete verb here.

items.explain: Runs and waves are both present tense.
items.hint: Make the second verb match runs.

items.prompt: Which verb fits the sentence?
items.visual: Last summer, our family ? a whale from the boat.

choices.why: Sees is present. Last summer is in the past.
Will see is future. Last summer is in the past.

items.explain: Last summer is in the past, so use saw. 🐋
items.hint: When was last summer?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that switches tense by mistake.

choices.t: The storm ended, and the sky cleared.
choices.why: Ended and cleared are both past. The tense matches.

choices.t: The storm ends, and the sky cleared.
The storm ends, and the sky clears.
choices.why: Ends and clears are both present. The tense matches.

items.explain: Ends is present, but cleared is past. That is a tense switch.
items.hint: Check if both verbs are in the same time.

items.prompt: Which word completes the pair?
items.visual: You can have either soup ? salad.

choices.why: Nor goes with neither, not either.
And goes with both, not either.

items.explain: Either goes with or: either soup or salad.
items.hint: Either and ____ are partners.

items.prompt: Which word completes the pair?
items.visual: Neither Sam ? Ben likes spiders.

choices.why: Or goes with either. Neither goes with nor.
And goes with both. Neither goes with nor.

items.explain: Neither goes with nor. Both start with n.
items.hint: Neither and nor both start with n.

items.prompt: Which word completes the pair?
items.visual: Both the cat ? the dog were asleep.

choices.why: Or goes with either, not both.
Nor goes with neither, not both.

items.explain: Both goes with and: both the cat and the dog.
items.hint: Both and ____ are partners.

items.prompt: Which words complete the pair?
items.visual: Zoe is not only kind ? funny.

choices.why: The partner of not only is but also.
Or goes with either, not with not only.

items.explain: Not only goes with but also. Zoe is not only kind but also funny.
items.hint: Not only ____ ____.

items.prompt: Which pair of words goes together correctly?

choices.why: Neither goes with nor, not or.
Both goes with and, not or.

items.explain: The correct pairs: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, not only ... but also.
items.hint: Which pair both start with n?

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that uses the pair correctly.

choices.t: Either Leo nor Mia will feed the fish.
choices.why: Either goes with or, not nor.

choices.t: Either Leo or Mia will feed the fish.
Both Leo or Mia will feed the fish.
choices.why: Both goes with and, not or.

items.explain: Either goes with or. Either Leo or Mia will feed the fish. 🐠
items.hint: Check that each pair has the right partner.

items.prompt: Which word completes the pair?
items.visual: Penguins can neither fly ? breathe underwater.

choices.why: And goes with both. Neither goes with nor.
But is not a partner for neither.

items.explain: Neither goes with nor. Penguins can neither fly nor breathe underwater. They swim, then come up for air. 🐧
items.hint: Neither and ____ both start with n.

items.prompt: Which word completes the pair?
items.visual: A platypus is both a mammal ? an egg layer.

choices.why: Or goes with either. Both goes with and.
Nor goes with neither. Both goes with and.

items.explain: Both goes with and. A platypus is both a mammal and an egg layer.
items.hint: Both and ____ are partners.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.visual: We stayed inside ? it was raining.

choices.why: Although shows a surprise. Staying in when it rains is not a surprise.
Unless means only if not. It does not fit here.

items.explain: because gives the reason. We stayed inside because it was raining.
items.hint: The rain is the reason.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? it was cold, Leo wore shorts.

choices.why: Cold weather is not a reason to wear shorts.
Since means because here. Cold weather is not a reason to wear shorts.

items.explain: Although shows a surprise. It was cold, but Leo still wore shorts.
items.hint: Does wearing shorts in the cold make sense, or is it a surprise?

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.visual: Plants will wilt ? they get enough water.

choices.why: Getting water does not make plants wilt.
Plants do not wilt when they get water.

items.explain: unless means "if not." Plants will wilt if they do not get enough water. 🌱
items.hint: What happens to plants with no water?

items.prompt: Tap the subordinating conjunction in this sentence.
items.visual: Since the bus was late, we walked to school.

choices.why: Bus is a noun. It names a thing.
Walked is a verb. It tells an action.

items.explain: Since starts the part that gives the reason: "since the bus was late."
items.hint: Look for a word like because, since, when, or although.

items.prompt: Tap the complex sentence.

choices.t: The bell rang, and the students lined up.
choices.why: This joins two sentences with and. That makes a compound sentence.

choices.t: When the bell rang, the students lined up.

choices.why: This is one simple sentence.

items.explain: "When the bell rang" cannot stand alone. It is joined to a full sentence, so it is a complex sentence.
items.hint: Look for when, because, since, although, or unless.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? the sun sets, many owls wake up.

choices.why: Unless means if not. Owls wake up at sunset, not "if the sun does not set."
Although shows a surprise. Owls waking at night is not a surprise.

items.explain: When tells the time. When the sun sets, many owls wake up. 🦉
items.hint: The sentence tells what happens at a certain time.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence with the comma in the right place.

choices.t: Because it snowed, school was closed.
Because it snowed school, was closed.
choices.why: The comma goes after snowed, at the end of the first part.

choices.t: Because, it snowed school was closed.
choices.why: The comma should not come right after because.

items.explain: When a sentence starts with because, put a comma at the end of that first part: "Because it snowed," ❄️
items.hint: Find where the "because" part ends.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.visual: ? Priya stayed up late reading, she was tired the next day.

choices.why: Although shows a surprise. Being tired after staying up late is not a surprise.
Unless means if not. It does not fit here.

items.explain: Here since means because. Since Priya stayed up late, she was tired. 📚
items.hint: Staying up late is the reason.

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: Honeybees make honey from flower nectar. A bee sips nectar and carries it back to the hive. There, other bees store it in wax cells. The bees fan their wings to dry out the nectar. Slowly, the thick, sweet liquid becomes honey.

choices.why: This is only one small detail.

choices.t: Honeybees carry nectar to the hive and turn it into honey.
Honey is the best food in the world.
choices.why: This is an opinion. The passage does not say it.

items.explain: The passage starts with "Honeybees make honey from flower nectar," then tells the steps. The best summary covers the whole process. 🍯
items.hint: Which choice covers the whole passage?

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: Water on Earth moves in a cycle. The Sun heats water in oceans and lakes, and it evaporates. The water vapor rises and cools into clouds. Then it falls back down as rain or snow. The water flows into rivers and oceans, and the cycle starts again.

choices.why: This is one detail. It leaves out most of the cycle.
The passage does not say this, and it misses the main idea.

choices.t: Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, and returns to oceans again and again.

items.explain: The first sentence says "Water on Earth moves in a cycle." The best summary names every step. 🌧️
items.hint: A good summary includes all the main steps.

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: The Arctic fox lives in one of the coldest places on Earth. Its thick fur keeps it warm. Its fur is white in winter to match the snow. In summer, the fur turns brown or gray. Even the bottoms of its paws are covered in fur.

choices.t: The Arctic fox has special fur that helps it live in a very cold place.
The Arctic fox has fur on its paws.
choices.why: This is one detail, not the whole passage.

choices.t: Arctic foxes live in hot deserts.
choices.why: The passage says they live in one of the coldest places on Earth.

items.explain: Every sentence tells how the fox's fur helps it in the cold. The best summary says that. 🦊
items.hint: What is almost every sentence about?

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: Scientists have sent robot rovers to explore Mars. The rovers have cameras that take pictures of the land. Some rovers can drill into rocks to study them. They send the pictures and data back to Earth. This helps scientists learn whether water once flowed on Mars.

choices.why: The passage does not talk about the color of Mars.

choices.t: Robot rovers explore Mars and send information back to help scientists learn about it.

choices.why: This is only one detail.

items.explain: The passage tells what rovers do on Mars and why: to help scientists learn. The best summary covers both. 🤖
items.hint: What do the rovers do, and why?

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Over many years, their hard skeletons pile up and form a reef. Reefs grow in warm, clear, shallow ocean water. Thousands of kinds of fish and sea animals live on reefs. That is why reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea.

choices.why: This is too general. It does not say anything about coral reefs.

choices.t: Coral reefs are ugly and boring.
choices.why: This is an opinion. The passage does not say it.

choices.t: Tiny coral animals build reefs, which are home to many kinds of sea life.

items.explain: The passage tells how reefs are built and that they are home to many animals. The best summary covers both. 🐠
items.hint: How are reefs made, and who lives there?

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.
items.visual: Orville and Wilbur Wright were brothers who loved to build things. For years, they tested gliders and studied how birds fly. In 1903, they built an airplane with an engine. Orville flew it for 12 seconds in North Carolina. It was the first successful powered airplane flight.

choices.t: After years of testing, the Wright brothers made the first powered airplane flight in 1903.

choices.why: This is one detail. It does not tell why the flight mattered.

choices.t: The Wright brothers liked birds more than planes.
choices.why: The passage does not say this. They studied birds to learn about flying.

items.explain: The passage tells how the brothers worked for years and then made "the first successful powered airplane flight." ✈️
items.hint: What big thing did the brothers do?

items.prompt: Tap the best summary of the passage.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that camels are built for sandy places?

People have ridden camels for thousands of years.

choices.why: This is true, but it is about energy, not about sand.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that octopuses are good at hiding?
items.visual: An octopus has eight arms. It can change the color of its skin in less than a second. It can make its skin look bumpy like a rock. An octopus has no bones. It eats crabs and clams.

choices.t: It can make its skin look bumpy like a rock.

items.explain: Looking like a rock helps an octopus blend in and hide. That proves the claim. 🐙

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that Mars is a very cold planet?
items.visual: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It looks red because of rusty dust. Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system. The average temperature on Mars is far below freezing. Mars has two small moons.

choices.t: It looks red because of rusty dust.
choices.why: This is about color, not temperature.

choices.t: The average temperature on Mars is far below freezing.

choices.why: This is about moons, not temperature.

items.explain: The claim is about cold. "Far below freezing" is the only sentence about temperature. 🔴
items.hint: Which sentence talks about temperature?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that Zoe is patient?
items.visual: Zoe wanted to see a hummingbird. She hung a feeder by the window. Day after day, she sat quietly and watched. A week went by with no birds. Finally, on the eighth day, a tiny green hummingbird came to drink.

She hung a feeder by the window.
choices.why: This shows what Zoe did first, but not that she waited calmly.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that trees help keep cities cool?
items.visual: Trees give homes to birds and squirrels. Their shade can make a street much cooler on a hot day. Trees also take in carbon dioxide from the air. In the fall, many trees drop their leaves. Some trees can live for hundreds of years.

choices.t: Trees give homes to birds and squirrels.

choices.t: In the fall, many trees drop their leaves.
choices.why: This is about leaves falling, not about keeping cool.

choices.t: Their shade can make a street much cooler on a hot day.

items.explain: The claim is about keeping cool. The sentence about shade making a street cooler proves it. 🌳
items.hint: Which sentence uses the word cooler?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that the telephone changed how people talked?
items.visual: Alexander Graham Bell got a patent for the telephone in 1876. Before phones, people sent letters that took days or weeks. With a phone, people could talk right away, even from far apart. Early phones were large and hung on walls. Today, many people carry phones in their pockets.

Early phones were large and hung on walls.

choices.t: Alexander Graham Bell got a patent for the telephone in 1876.
